I’m Ali, a YouTuber, podcaster, author of New York Times and Sunday Times bestseller, Feel-Good Productivity, and ex-Doctor working in London, UK.

This method from Cal Newport helped me figure out what I wanted to do with my life.

It's called values-centric lifestyle-based career planning. The idea is simple: work backwards from the lifestyle you want.

A lot of us think "I did a degree in X, so my only options are A, B, or C."

But actually, start by asking yourself what kind of life you want.

📅 What would your ideal week look like?

💸 What would you be doing if money were no object?

Most people get meaning from work. It's just that you'd probably be doing work you enjoy. So what would that look like?

Then based on that, figure out what kind of career would actually facilitate that lifestyle.

This advice really resonated with me when I was in med school.

🔍 Start with the life you want, then figure out the career that gets you there.

Someone asked: "My son just turned 22. What advice would you give him?"

Firstly, I don't give advice to people who aren't asking for it. So I probably wouldn't force my advice down your 22-year-old son's throat.

But if a 22-year-old came up to me and asked for general life advice, I'd say this.

When you're 22, you don't have a lot of experience in many things. You probably did something at university, maybe had some hobbies or side hustles, but you've got a fairly narrow range of stuff you've actually tried.

(P.S. Comment FOUNDATIONS below for my free 7-lesson course on how to build a $100k/year business)

So from 22 to 25, just try loads of things. Internships. Working for a small business. Random hobbies and side projects. Try learning the skills to make money independently on the internet.

And make sure you are creating more than you are consuming. Creating doesn't have to mean content. It can mean any form of making stuff and putting it out into the world.

Paul Graham has a great essay about finding work you love, and one of his guiding principles is "always be producing." The people who stumble into interesting careers tend to produce a lot. Most 22-year-olds I know spend 10 hours a day consuming content other people made.

Shift from consumer to creator. Try enough things and you'll eventually find the one where you're like "oh, I actually enjoyed that more than the others”, then narrow it down from there.

As Naval Ravikant says, find the thing that feels like play to you but looks like work to other people 🧙

If you have a friend who is chronically single, send them this book 👀

It's called How to Not Die Alone by @loganury.

She's a behavioural scientist turned dating coach and she's now basically the head of behavioural science at Hinge.

The book takes insights from behavioural science and applies them to the world of dating, and it's genuinely really good.

I read it about four years ago, right when I first met my wife ❤️ She actually recommended it to me on our first date. I read the book, and we are now married. So yeah, it works 😂

I asked Alex @Hormozi how he'd make $100k a year doing what he loves.

His answer was basically, find one super valuable service you can do for a business, charge them $100K for it, then figure out what to do with the other 364 days of the year 😂

(If you want the full podcast episode, comment ALEX and I'll send it to you)

What hit me was how casually he said it. He wasn't born with the skills to charge that much. He learned them over time to the point where hundreds of thousands feels like nothing.

It completely reset my bar for what's reasonable. Growing up, my parents were doctors, everyone I knew was a doctor. In the UK, doctor earnings basically cap out around $100k. That was all I could imagine as a reasonable income.

But after years of being an entrepreneur, running a business that does millions in revenue and profit, having friends who spend hundreds of thousands a month on ads profitably - you start to realise that $100k is actually not that much money. Provided you've learned the skills for it not to be.

And the nice thing about skills is that everything that's a skill can be learned. If something feels like "a lot of money", that's just a skill issue and an exposure issue 💡
